summary: A short addendum to RFC 987, which maps between X.400 and RFC 822 mail. It was a proposed protocol and asked for discussion. It updates RFC 987 and was updated by RFC 1138 and RFC 1148, and replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156.

eli5.summary: It is a small correction note added to the translation guide between two different email systems.

subtitle: Corrections and additions to the X.400 to RFC 822 mail mapping defined in RFC 987.

tldr.problem: RFC 987, which maps between X.400 and RFC 822 mail, had typographical errors, left the order of repeated name components unclear, and was inflexible when parts of a name such as Organisation or PRMD were omitted.
tldr.mechanism: The addendum lists errata, fixes the ordering of Organisational Units and Domain Defined Attributes, adds an "@" symbol for explicitly omitted components, and defines a new Appendix F with table formats for address mapping.
tldr.outcome: It was a proposed protocol that carries equal weight to RFC 987. It was updated by RFC 1138 and RFC 1148 and replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156.

today: RFC 1026 is obsoleted by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156, and was updated by RFC 1138 and RFC 1148. It amends RFC 987.

sections.title: Errata and Status
sections.content:
This addendum lists a number of additions and corrections to RFC 987, also known as Mailgroup Note 19. It carries equal weight to the original specification, which must be used when the mapping is performed on the Internet or in the UK Academic Community. The mapping may also be used within the RARE community in Europe.

The errata fix specific slips: in section 4.6.4 replace ".." with ".", in section 4.2.4 correct some section references, and in section 5.2 replace "1 mailbox", "1 msg-id" and "1 encoded-type" with the "1#" forms.
sections.eli5: It is a list of typo fixes for the guide, plus a note that the fixes count just as much as the guide itself.

sections.title: Component Ordering
sections.content:
Ordering of O/R name components is mostly not significant for this mapping. But Organisational Units and Domain Defined Attributes are a SEQUENCE in P1.ORName, so their order may matter. The addendum fixes order in three places.

  • In the text encoding (std-orname) used in the local part of an RFC 822 address, the most significant component must be on the right-hand side.
  • For Organisational Units, the first OU in the SEQUENCE is the most significant.
  • For Domain Defined Attributes, the first one in the SEQUENCE is the most significant.

This ordering is mandatory for the mapping, but it has no implications for ordering significance within X.400.
sections.eli5: When a name has several pieces in a row, the rules now say which piece is the biggest one, so everyone writes them in the same order.

sections.title: Omitted Components
sections.content:
Implementing RFC 987 proved a little inflexible for some naming strategies, particularly where Organisation or PRMD is omitted. A sentence in section 4.2.1 of RFC 987 is removed, and the addendum introduces the concept of explicit missing components into the symmetrical mapping.

A domain may be associated with an omitted attribute alongside several present ones, and when inserting components lower in the hierarchy the omitted value is skipped. In the RFC's example, "GMD.DFN" is associated with C=DE, ADMD=DBP, PRMD=GMD and an omitted organisation, so "ZI.GMD.DFN" maps with OU=ZI. Null values are treated separately from omitted attributes.

To represent this, the dmn-orname syntax is extended so a value may be the symbol @, meaning an omitted attribute.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a middle piece of an address is missing. A special mark, @, now says "skip this one on purpose".

sections.title: Appendix F: Address Mapping Tables
sections.content:
A new Appendix F defines a table syntax for the association between the domain and X.400 name spaces. It is written so it can also suit domain nameservices. The mapping is not symmetric, so a separate table is given for each direction, and when several matches are possible the longest match should be used.

Rules for dmn-orname: only C, ADMD, PRMD, O and OU may be used; components are strictly ordered with the most significant on the right; and no components may be omitted from the hierarchy, though it may end at any level, with "@" for a mapping to an omitted component.

For domain to X.400 the entry is the domain syntax, a "#", the dmn-orname and a trailing "#" (kept for clarity because values can end in blanks). For X.400 to domain the order is reversed.
sections.eli5: Appendix F is a lookup table for turning one kind of address into the other, with one table for each direction.
